name: Mars Global Surveyor
significance: Mars Global Surveyor set out to answer a question left open since the failed Mars Observer mission four years earlier: what does the Martian surface actually look like at global scale, and could it reveal whether liquid water ever -- or still -- shaped the planet? Launched direct to Mars on a Delta II 7925 and inserted into orbit using a pioneering aerobraking technique that traded propellant mass for months of careful atmospheric-drag passes, it became the first fully successful Mars orbiter since Viking. Its laser altimeter produced the first high-resolution global topographic map of Mars, while its camera discovered hundreds of geologically young gully features whose morphology strongly suggested recent flows of liquid water. Operating for nearly a decade -- five times its planned mission life -- MGS also scouted landing sites for the Spirit, Opportunity, and Phoenix missions before contact was lost in November 2006, leaving a legacy still cited as one of the most scientifically productive Mars missions ever flown.
statusNote: Direct Earth->Mars transfer, no gravity assists. Mars orbit insertion 1997-09-11, then months of aerobraking (repeated atmospheric-drag passes) to reach its final circular mapping orbit while conserving propellant -- the first fully successful use of this technique at another planet. Operated for nearly a decade before an error while reorienting a solar panel triggered a power/thermal fault; contact was lost 2006-11-02, and NASA declared the mission ended 2007-01-28. The spacecraft remains in stable Mars orbit.
